findings.source_passage: "Your language, Tuppence, your language! They're very particular at the National Gallery. Government show, you know. And do remember, as I have pointed out to you before, that as a clergyman's daughter----" "I ought to be on the stage!"
findings.source_locator: After Tommy reveals two answers, before they open the envelopes
findings.why_it_matters: This running gag—the clergyman's daughter joke—is a signature Christie comic motif that recurs across the novel and establishes the banter register between Tommy and Tuppence; its absence removes a key voice beat.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the 'clergyman's daughter / ought to be on the stage' exchange verbatim or near-verbatim; it is short and self-contained.

findings.source_passage: "That is not what I intended to say. But if you are sure that you have enjoyed to the full the reaction of joy after despair with which I have kindly provided you free of charge, let us get down to our mail, as the saying goes."
findings.why_it_matters: This line is prosodically distinctive Christie dialogue—mock-formal, self-aware, comedically inflated—and is the payoff of the letter-withholding scene; its compression to a bare transition erases the scene's tonal identity.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore this speech in full or keep the key clause ('enjoyed to the full the reaction of joy after despair…provided free of charge') to preserve the ironic register.

findings.source_passage: "Ha!" said Tommy. "Do I smell a Boche? Or only an American millionaire of unfortunate ancestry? At all events we'll call at lunch-time. It's a good time--frequently leads to free food for two."
findings.why_it_matters: The draft keeps 'free food for two' but drops the arch 'Do I smell a Boche? Or only an American millionaire of unfortunate ancestry?'—a period-register line that characterises Tommy's voice and the novel's post-war comic tone.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the 'Boche / American millionaire of unfortunate ancestry' phrasing; it is short and period-distinctive.

findings.source_passage: "Most of the Peace propaganda during the war was originated and financed by him. His spies are everywhere." "A naturalized German?" asked Tommy. "On the contrary, I have every reason to believe he is an Englishman."
findings.source_locator: Carter's exposition of Mr. Brown, after 'master criminal of this age'
findings.why_it_matters: The 'A naturalized German? / On the contrary, an Englishman' exchange is interpretively important: it plants the key misdirection about Mr. Brown's nationality, which matters for the novel's mystery structure; its omission removes a narratively load-bearing beat.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore Tommy's question and Carter's answer about Brown's nationality, plus the 'Peace propaganda' detail, which foreshadows later revelations.

findings.source_passage: "She was an orphan, and had been what we should call over here a pupil teacher in a small school out West. Her passport had been made out for Paris, where she was going to join the staff of a hospital."
findings.source_locator: Carter's account of Jane Finn's antecedents
findings.why_it_matters: Jane Finn's background details—orphan, pupil teacher, school out West, hospital volunteer—give her the period-specific, sympathetic colouring that makes her disappearance feel real; stripping them to a bare 'she vanished' flattens characterisation.
findings.suggested_fix: Add one sentence restoring 'orphan… pupil teacher… small school out West… going to join a hospital' to preserve the characterisation of Jane Finn.

summary: Three medium-severity voice losses (the clergyman's-daughter gag, Tommy's mock-formal 'joy after despair' speech, and the 'naturalized German / Englishman' exchange) plus a fourth medium-severity interpretive omission (Brown's nationality misdirection) trigger a regenerate verdict.
